title: These and These: When Movements Differ
hookLine: Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative rabbis perform same-sex weddings; Orthodox rabbis do not
carry: these and these: argue honestly, share the table

cards: Two schools of rabbis, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, disagreed about marriage law. Not about flowers or music: about who was permitted to marry whom. The stakes were high.
By one school's rules, some marriages the other allowed should not have happened. And yet the Mishnah records something striking.

The house of Shammai did not hold back from marrying into families of the house of Hillel, and the house of Hillel did not hold back from the house of Shammai. They disagreed, and they still married each other's children.

teach.h: SAID PLAINLY: WHO DOES, WHO DOESN'T.
teach.b: Here is today's difference, said plainly. Rabbis in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements perform weddings for same-sex couples; their movements allow it, though an individual rabbi may still decline.
Orthodox rabbis do not. Orthodox rabbis hold that Torah law, as their tradition reads it, does not allow such a marriage, and they keep to that reading.

The Conservative movement reached its answer through its own process of Jewish legal reasoning. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism understand tradition as something each generation carries forward and reshapes.
Each works from Torah and the rabbis, takes the question seriously, and arrives in a different place.
You met these and these back in your first year.
The Talmud tells of a long argument between Hillel's school and Shammai's, until a heavenly voice says both are the words of the living God, and the practical law follows Hillel. Why Hillel?
Because his students were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's view alongside their own, even putting it first. In Hebrew: elu va'elu, these and these. On an ordinary day, that looks like this.
Families sometimes span more than one movement. A guest at a wedding follows that community's customs.

teach.h: ARGUE, AND STILL SHARE A TABLE.
teach.b: People can hold their own view firmly and still describe another's accurately, without mockery.

teach.h: THESE AND THESE: WHEN MOVEMENTS DIFFER.
teach.b: This lesson doesn't settle the question; it describes who says what. The old rabbis left a model: argue honestly, teach the other side fairly, and keep coming to each other's tables.

how: Rabbis in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements officiate at same-sex weddings; Orthodox rabbis do not, holding to their reading of Jewish law.

games.q: you're of the house of Hillel. the house of Shammai rules differently from you on marriage law. a match is proposed with one of their families. what do you do?
o: refuse: their rulings differ from yours.
go ahead: the two houses married into each other's families.
demand they change their rulings first.
games.why: the Mishnah says neither house held back from marrying into the other, even while they disagreed.

practice: Bring to mind a community not your own, a congregation, a family, a group of friends, that does something differently from the way you would, and let a few real faces from it come.
Notice any urge to win the argument and let it sit; look instead for one thing in them you can honestly respect, their care or their seriousness, and hold it for a while.

wordCard.voice: Communities differ: on same-sex weddings, and on much else, Jewish movements answer differently, each from its reading of the tradition. Today's word.
